### "Centre of New Zealand" monument

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: \"Centre of New Zealand\" monument")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Geographical_centre_nelson.jpg/250px-Geographical_centre_nelson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Geographical_centre_nelson.jpg)

The marker at the "Centre of New Zealand"

Nelson has a monument on Botanical Hill, near the centre of the city. The walk to this is called the "_Centre of New Zealand walk_". Despite the name, this monument does not mark the actual geographic centre of New Zealand.

Instead, the monument marks the "zero, zero" point to which the first geodetic surveys of New Zealand were referenced. These surveys were started in the 1870s by John Spence Browning, the Chief Surveyor for Nelson. From this 360-degree viewpoint, survey marks in neighbouring regions (including Wellington in the North Island) could be [triangulated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangulation "Triangulation") and the local surveys connected.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-42)

In 1962, Ian Reilly from the now defunct [Department of Scientific and Industrial Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Scientific_and_Industrial_Research_(New_Zealand) "Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (New Zealand)") calculated the geographic centre of New Zealand (including Stewart Island and some smaller islands in addition to the North and South Island, but excluding the [Chathams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_Islands "Chatham Islands")) to be in a forest in [Spooners Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spooner's_Range,_New_Zealand?action=edit&redlink=1 "Spooner's Range, New Zealand (page does not exist)")35 mi (56 kilometres) southwest of Nelson at [41°30′S 172°50′E / 41.500°S 172.833°E / -41.500; 172.833 (Geographical Centre of New Zealand)](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Nelson,_New_Zealand&params=41_30_S_172_50_E_region:NZ_type:landmark&title=Geographical+Centre+of+New+Zealand).[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-43)

Owing to the coarse nature of the underlying data (use of rectangular areas of 7.5 minutes of arc on each side), the centre calculated by Reilly has quite large error margins. Recalculating the result with more modern and accurate data shows the geographic centre of New Zealand is approximately 60 km southwest of Nelson, in the Big Bush Conservation Area north of [Saint Arnaud, New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Arnaud,_New_Zealand "Saint Arnaud, New Zealand").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-44)

## Government

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Government")]

### Local

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Local")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Nelson_City_Council_Building.JPG/250px-Nelson_City_Council_Building.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nelson_City_Council_Building.JPG)

The Nelson City Council building in 2012

As a [unitary authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_authority "Unitary authority"), the [Nelson City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_City_Council "Nelson City Council") has the combined responsibilities and functions of both a [territorial (local)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_authorities_of_New_Zealand "Territorial authorities of New Zealand") and [regional council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_New_Zealand "Regions of New Zealand"). This is different from most other local authorities in New Zealand. More often, a regional council is a separate organisation with several territorial authorities (city or district councils) within its borders. Other unitary authorities are the [Auckland Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland_Council "Auckland Council"), [Gisborne District Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gisborne_District_Council "Gisborne District Council"), [Marlborough District Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Region "Marlborough Region"), [Tasman District Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasman_District_Council "Tasman District Council") and the [Chatham Islands Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_Islands_Council "Chatham Islands Council").

The Nelson City Council holds elections for the [mayor of Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Nelson,_New_Zealand "Mayor of Nelson, New Zealand") and 12 councillors under the [STV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_Transferable_Voting "Single Transferable Voting") electoral system every three years. As of 12 October 2025, the mayor is [Nick Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Smith_(New_Zealand_politician) "Nick Smith (New Zealand politician)").

Nelson City has a coat of arms, obtained in 1958 from the [College of Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Arms "College of Arms") to mark the centenary of Nelson as a city. The [blazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blazon "Blazon") of the arms is:

"Barry wavy Argent and Azure a Cross Flory Sable on a Chief also Azure a Mitre proper And for the Crest on a Wreath of the Colours Issuant from a Mural Crown proper a Lion rampant Gules holding between the fore paws a Sun in splendour or. The supporters on the dexter side a Huia Bird and on the sinister side a Kotuku both proper."
Motto "_Palmam qui meruit ferat_" (Let him who has earned it bear the palm). This motto is the same as that of [Lord Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Nelson "Horatio Nelson").

### National

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: National")]

Nelson is covered by the [Nelson general electorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_(New_Zealand_electorate) "Nelson (New Zealand electorate)"), and the [Te Tai Tonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Tai_Tonga "Te Tai Tonga") Māori electorate, which covers the entire South Island and part of [Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington "Wellington") in the North Island. Since the [2023 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_general_election "2023 New Zealand general election"), Nelson is held by [Rachel Boyack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachel_Boyack "Rachel Boyack") of the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party "New Zealand Labour Party"), and Te Tai Tonga by [Tākuta Ferris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C4%81kuta_Ferris "Tākuta Ferris") of [Te Pāti Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori "Te Pāti Māori").

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Economy")]

The Nelson economy (and that of the neighbouring [Tasman District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasman_District "Tasman District")) is based on the 'big five' industries; seafood, horticulture, forestry, farming and tourism.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-54) Port Nelson[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-55) is the biggest fishing port in [Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia "Australasia"). There are also a range of growth industries, including art and craft, aviation, [engineering technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_technology "Engineering technology"), and information technology. The region was sixth in terms of GDP growth in the 2007–10 period.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-stuff.co.nz-56)

The combined sub-national GDP of Nelson and Tasman District was estimated at $3.4 billion in 2010, 1.8% of New Zealand's national GDP.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-stuff.co.nz-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-57)

The Nelson Regional Development Agency is an economic development agency for Nelson and the Tasman District.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-58)

Some of the region's largest companies and employers are:

*   [Helicopters (NZ)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicopters_(NZ) "Helicopters (NZ)") has its headquarters and maintenance base at [Nelson Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Airport_(New_Zealand) "Nelson Airport (New Zealand)").
*   Japanese automobile manufacturer [Honda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honda "Honda") has its New Zealand distribution centre in the Whakatu Industrial Estate in [Stoke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke,_New_Zealand "Stoke, New Zealand").
*   Beverage company [McCashins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCashins_Brewery "McCashins Brewery") has a [microbrewery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microbrewery "Microbrewery") in Stoke.
*   SeaDragon Marine Oils[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-59) has a fish oil refinery in Annesbrook.
*   The [Cawthron Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cawthron_Institute "Cawthron Institute") has a research facility in [The Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wood,_New_Zealand "The Wood, New Zealand").
*   Food manufacturer the [Talley's Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talley's_Group "Talley's Group") has processing facilities at [Port Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Nelson,_New_Zealand "Port Nelson, New Zealand").
*   New Zealand King Salmon processes [Chinook salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_salmon "Chinook salmon") at its factory in [Annesbrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annesbrook "Annesbrook").
*   [Pic's Peanut Butter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pic's_Peanut_Butter "Pic's Peanut Butter") is made in its Stoke factory.

Former regional airline [Air Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Nelson "Air Nelson") had its headquarters and maintenance base at Nelson Airport.

In 2013, Nelson Mayor [Aldo Miccio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldo_Miccio "Aldo Miccio") worked on a proposal that would see Australian [call centres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_centres "Call centres") for companies such as [Gen-i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gen-i "Gen-i") and [Xero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xero_(software) "Xero (software)") relocated to Nelson. The plan was in response to Australian companies moving call and contact centres out of Asia because their Australian customers preferred English-speaking centres. If the plan was successful, Miccio expected 100 to 300 jobs paying NZ$50,000-plus in the first year to be created in Nelson.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-60)

### Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Tourism")]

Nelson is a gateway for tourists and visitors exploring the [Abel Tasman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Tasman_National_Park "Abel Tasman National Park"), [Kahurangi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kahurangi_National_Park "Kahurangi National Park"), and [Nelson Lakes National Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Lakes_National_Park "Nelson Lakes National Park"), and the [Great Taste Trail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Taste_Trail "Great Taste Trail"), and popular walks such as the [Abel Tasman Coast Track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Tasman_Coast_Track "Abel Tasman Coast Track"), and [Heaphy Track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaphy_Track "Heaphy Track").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-61)

It is a centre for both [ecotourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecotourism "Ecotourism") and [adventure tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure_travel "Adventure travel") and has a high reputation among [caving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave "Cave") enthusiasts due to several prominent cave systems around [Takaka Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takaka_Hill "Takaka Hill") and the [Wharepapa / Arthur Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wharepapa_/_Arthur_Range "Wharepapa / Arthur Range"), including the [Nettlebed Cave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nettlebed_Cave "Nettlebed Cave") and some of the largest and deepest explored caverns in the Southern Hemisphere.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Electricity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: Electricity")]

The Nelson City Municipal Electricity Department (MED) established the city's public electricity supply in 1923, with electricity generated by a coal-fired power station at Wakefield Quay. The city was connected to the newly commissioned [Cobb hydroelectric power station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobb_Power_Station "Cobb Power Station") in 1944 and to the rest of the South Island grid in 1958. The grid connection saw the Wakefield Quay power station was relegated to standby duty before being decommissioned in 1964.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Nelson_Electricity_Ltd,_New_Zealand-108)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-109)

Today, Nelson Electricity operates the local distribution network in the former MED area, which covers the CBD and inner suburbs, while Network Tasman operates the local distribution network in the outer suburbs (including Stoke, Tāhunanui and Atawhai) and the nearby rural areas.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Nelson_Electricity_Ltd,_New_Zealand-108)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-110)

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: Transport")]

### Air transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nelson,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=41 "Edit section: Air transport")]

[Nelson Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Airport_(New_Zealand) "Nelson Airport (New Zealand)") is at [Annesbrook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annesbrook "Annesbrook"), an industrial suburb southwest of the central city. It operates a single terminal and 1,347-metre (4,419-foot) runway. About a million passengers use the airport annually and it was the [fifth-busiest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_New_Zealand "List of the busiest airports in New Zealand") airport in New Zealand by passenger numbers in 2024. It is primarily used for domestic flights, with regular flights to and from [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland"), [Christchurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch "Christchurch"), [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_New_Zealand "Hamilton, New Zealand"), [Kāpiti Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C4%81piti_Coast "Kāpiti Coast"), [Palmerston North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmerston_North "Palmerston North") and [Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington "Wellington"). [Sounds Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sounds_Air "Sounds Air") offers flights to and from Wellington. In 2006, it received restricted international airport status to facilitate small private jets.

The airport was home to [Air Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Nelson "Air Nelson"), which operated and maintained New Zealand's largest domestic airline fleet, and is now merged into [Air New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_New_Zealand "Air New Zealand"). It was also the headquarters of [Origin Pacific Airways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_Pacific_Airways "Origin Pacific Airways") until its collapse in 2006.

In February 2018, the approach road to the airport was flooded when the adjoining Jenkins Creek burst its banks during a storm that brought king tides and strong winds. The airport was closed for about one hour.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-111) In 2022, the NZ SeaRise programme identified Nelson airport as an area of particular vulnerability to [sea level rise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level_rise_in_New_Zealand "Sea level rise in New Zealand"), with a projected subsidence of 5 millimetres (0.20 in) per year.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Bradnock-2022-112) The airport's chief executive said that the proposed runway extension would be planned around the latest sea level rise forecast, and that the airport was "here to stay", despite the concerns over the threats posed by sea level rise.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Bradnock-2022-112)

**Blenheim** ([/ˈ b l ɛ n ɪ m/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_BLEN-im_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_language "Māori language"): _Waiharakeke_[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-2)) is the most populous [town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town "Town") in the [region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_New_Zealand "Regions of New Zealand") of [Marlborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_District "Marlborough District"), in the north east of the [South Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island "South Island") of [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"). It has an estimated population of 29,800 as of June 2025.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-NZ_population_data_2018-1) The surrounding [Marlborough wine region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_wine_region "Marlborough wine region") is well known as the centre of the [New Zealand wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_wine "New Zealand wine") industry. It enjoys one of New Zealand's sunniest [climates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate "Climate"), with warm, relatively dry summers and cool, crisp winters.

Blenheim is named after the [Battle of Blenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Blenheim "Battle of Blenheim") (1704) in the [War of the Spanish Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession "War of the Spanish Succession"), where troops led by [John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Churchill,_1st_Duke_of_Marlborough "John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough") defeated a combined French and [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria") force. The New Zealand [Ministry for Culture and Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_for_Culture_and_Heritage "Ministry for Culture and Heritage") gives a translation of "[flax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phormium_tenax "Phormium tenax") stream" for the town's Māori name, _Waiharakeke_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Wikipedia-blenheim.jpg/250px-Wikipedia-blenheim.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikipedia-blenheim.jpg)

"Kia Ora Welcome to Blenheim"

The sheltered coastal bays of Marlborough supported a small [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people "Māori people") population possibly as early as the 12th century. Archaeological evidence dates Polynesian human remains uncovered at Wairau Bar to the 13th century. The rich sea and bird life of the area would easily have supported such small communities. As the Māori population of the area increased, they developed the land to sustain the growing population. In the early 1700s canals and waterways were dug among the natural river courses, allowing for the first forms of farming in the area including that of fish and native water fowl. A total of approximately 18 km of channels are known to have been excavated before the arrival of European settlers. Māori in the Marlborough Region also cultivated crops, including kūmara ([sweet potato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_potato "Sweet potato")).

The area is also home to the first serious clash of arms between Māori and the British settlers after the signing of the [Treaty of Waitangi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi "Treaty of Waitangi"). The [Wairau Affray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wairau_Affray "Wairau Affray") which occurred in what is now the village of [Tuamarina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuamarina "Tuamarina").

The settlement was originally known to Europeans as _The Beaver_ or _Beaverton_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-4) due to its frequent flooding.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-5)

Although the early history of Marlborough was closely associated with the [Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Province "Nelson Province") settlement, the people of Marlborough desired independence from Nelson. In 1859, nineteen years after the original Nelson settlement, the request of Marlborough settlers was granted, and Marlborough became a [separate province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Province "Marlborough Province"). Although gold was discovered in the province in the early 1860s the resulting boom did not last, and while the gold rush helped to expand the region, it was the development of pastoralism which provided the greatest long-term benefits. Marlborough squatters developed huge sheep runs that dominated the countryside, rivalling [Canterbury's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury,_New_Zealand "Canterbury, New Zealand") sheep stations in size and wealth.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Blenheim_New_Zeland.jpg/250px-Blenheim_New_Zeland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blenheim_New_Zeland.jpg)

View from above looking north from Blenheim

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Blenheim%2C_NZ.jpg/250px-Blenheim%2C_NZ.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blenheim,_NZ.jpg)

The Taylor River in central Blenheim

Situated on the Wairau Plain, the town is mostly flat with only its southernmost fringe rising to the base of the Wither Hills. As the plain is surrounded by mountains on all but the eastern flank, which is open to Cook Strait, it is relatively well protected from the frequent southerly weather fronts occurring during winters. The area does however experience some high wind events during the course of the year, especially from the west where the wind is funnelled down the [Wairau Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wairau_Valley "Wairau Valley") directly at the town. Open and exposed areas in and around Blenheim are also hit quite hard by winds blowing inland from Cook Strait. Blenheim sits at the confluence of the [Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_River_(Marlborough,_New_Zealand) "Taylor River (Marlborough, New Zealand)") and [Ōpaoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Cpaoa_River "Ōpaoa River") rivers. It is in a tectonically active zone and experiences several (usually small) earthquakes each year. The boundary between the Pacific plate (on which Blenheim sits) and the Indo-Australian plate passes just north of Blenheim. It lies east of Renwick, and just south of Spring Creek.

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Climate")]

The climate is generally very settled, largely due to the [rain shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow") effect of the mountain ranges to the west which [shelter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foehn_effect "Foehn effect") Blenheim from the heaviest of rains that hit the western part of the South Island.

Summers are typically warm, dry and sunny. Winter mornings are cool and frosty. Snowfall is rare as the town is sheltered from cold southerly weather by the mountain ranges to the south. Rainfall and humidity is highest in winter and early spring, between June and October. The town's average annual rainfall is a little more than 700mm, with 81.5 precipitation days.

Thunderstorms are an uncommon occurrence due to the sheltered climate. There is a higher likelihood in summer, when afternoon heating can generate a buildup of clouds above the ranges.

The highest recorded temperature is 37.8°C, recorded on 7 February 1973.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-6) The lowest is −8.8°C.

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Demographics")]

The Blenheim urban area, which Stats NZ describes as a medium urban area, covers 27.46 km 2 (10.60 sq mi) and incorporates thirteen statistical areas.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Area-11) It had an estimated population of 29,800 as of June 2025,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-NZ_population_data_2018-1) with a population density of 1,085 people per km 2.

Blenheim had a population of 28,788 in the [2023 New Zealand census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_census "2023 New Zealand census"), an increase of 1,140 people (4.1%) since the [2018 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_Zealand_census "2018 New Zealand census"), and an increase of 3,546 people (14.0%) since the [2013 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_New_Zealand_census "2013 New Zealand census"). There were 14,043 males, 14,652 females, and 93 people of [other genders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-binary_gender "Non-binary gender") in 11,583 dwellings.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-14) 2.7% of people identified as [LGBTIQ+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ "LGBTQ"). The median age was 43.2 years (compared with 38.1 years nationally). There were 4,917 people (17.1%) aged under 15 years, 4,467 (15.5%) aged 15 to 29, 12,561 (43.6%) aged 30 to 64, and 6,843 (23.8%) aged 65 or older.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Census_2023-12)

People could identify as more than one ethnicity. The results were 82.5% [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_New_Zealanders "European New Zealanders") ([Pākehā](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C4%81keh%C4%81 "Pākehā")); 15.0% [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people "Māori people"); 4.9% [Pasifika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasifika_New_Zealanders "Pasifika New Zealanders"); 7.4% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_New_Zealanders "Asian New Zealanders"); 2.1% Middle Eastern, Latin American and African New Zealanders (MELAA); and 2.7% other, which includes people giving their ethnicity as "New Zealander". English was spoken by 96.9%, Māori by 2.8%, Samoan by 1.1%, and other languages by 11.2%. No language could be spoken by 1.8% (e.g. too young to talk). [New Zealand Sign Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Sign_Language "New Zealand Sign Language") was known by 0.5%. The percentage of people born overseas was 21.4, compared with 28.8% nationally.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Census_2023-12)

Religious affiliations were 33.0% [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_New_Zealand "Christianity in New Zealand"), 1.1% [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism_in_New_Zealand "Hinduism in New Zealand"), 0.4% [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_New_Zealand "Islam in New Zealand"), 0.6% [Māori religious beliefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_religious_beliefs "Māori religious beliefs"), 0.9% [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism_in_New_Zealand "Buddhism in New Zealand"), 0.3% [New Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Age "New Age"), 0.1% [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism_in_New_Zealand "Judaism in New Zealand"), and 1.2% other religions. People who answered that they had [no religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion_in_New_Zealand "Irreligion in New Zealand") were 54.8%, and 7.8% of people did not answer the census question.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Census_2023-12)

Of those at least 15 years old, 4,212 (17.6%) people had a bachelor's or higher degree, 12,951 (54.3%) had a post-high school certificate or diploma, and 6,711 (28.1%) people exclusively held high school qualifications. The median income was $38,700, compared with $41,500 nationally. 1,782 people (7.5%) earned over $100,000 compared to 12.1% nationally. The employment status of those at least 15 was 11,835 (49.6%) full-time, 3,318 (13.9%) part-time, and 420 (1.8%) unemployed.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-Census_2023-12)

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Economy")]

The town's economy is based on agricultural services, with [pastoral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoral "Pastoral") and [horticultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horticultural "Horticultural") farming providing a major source of income. Historically, sheep farming, dairying, and wheat and barley were the major activities in the area. Marlborough's first commercial grape vines were planted in 1973, and since then [viticulture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viticulture "Viticulture") has become the dominant industry in the region; employment is derived not only from the production of wine, but also from 'wine tourism' in the area. [Olive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive "Olive") growing has also gained some importance in recent years. Despite being located several kilometres inland, maritime industries are also important sources of employment for Blenheim. [Lake Grassmere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Grassmere "Lake Grassmere") has New Zealand's only [salt works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt "Salt"), producing 50% of the country's total salt requirement. [Fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing "Fishing") and [mussel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mussel "Mussel") farming are also important in the region.

### Wine production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Wine production")]

Main article: [Marlborough wine region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_wine_region "Marlborough wine region")

Viticulture also has a very large impact on the local economy both directly, by way of employment and servicing required, and also by way of 'wine tourism'. The local cellars attracted hundreds of thousands of domestic and international tourists every year. The area also hosts the annual [Marlborough Wine & Food Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Wine_&_Food_Festival?action=edit&redlink=1 "Marlborough Wine & Food Festival (page does not exist)"). The [Marlborough wine region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_wine_region "Marlborough wine region") is now New Zealand's largest, and receives worldwide recognition for its [Sauvignon Blanc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauvignon_Blanc "Sauvignon Blanc") wines.

With its growing international critical recognition, much of the Marlborough wine industry has come to be dominated by large firms, owned by major New Zealand companies or offshore investors. There are over 50 vineyards near Blenheim. Agricultural land prices in the [Wairau Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wairau_Valley "Wairau Valley") increased dramatically in the 1990s and 2000s.

## Lifestyle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Lifestyle")]

The sunny, pleasant [climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate "Climate") has long attracted people to the region, as holiday-makers or as permanent [settlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlers "Settlers"). The region is especially popular among retired people, as well as people seeking an alternative lifestyle. Rapid population growth and other factors though have led to a contemporary chronic shortage of affordable housing for low and middle income earners.

The Marlborough Region has a wide range of predominantly outdoor [leisure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leisure "Leisure") activities and the relaxed lifestyle and the flourishing wine and [gourmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gourmet "Gourmet") food industry in Marlborough are enjoyed by both locals and visitors alike.

## Events and points of interest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Events and points of interest")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Blenheim2.JPG/250px-Blenheim2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blenheim2.JPG)

[Seymour Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seymour_Square,_Blenheim "Seymour Square, Blenheim"), the main square of Blenheim

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Seymour_sq%2C_Blenheim.JPG/250px-Seymour_sq%2C_Blenheim.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seymour_sq,_Blenheim.JPG)

Seymour Sq, Blenheim in early spring 2012

[Omaka Aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaka_Aerodrome "Omaka Aerodrome"), south of the town centre, is the setting for the two-yearly [Classic Fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Fighters "Classic Fighters") Marlborough airshow. With a large emphasis on aircraft of World War One, it has been held since 2001.

Seymour Square and Pollard Park are two of the town centres main attractions for walks and general tourism. Seymour Square is an open public area in the centre, containing the War Memorial and Clock Tower, unveiled in 1928, classified as a "Category I" ("places of 'special or outstanding historical or cultural heritage significance or value'") historic place by [Heritage New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_New_Zealand "Heritage New Zealand").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-28) The Square was named after Henry Seymour.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-29) Pollard Park is a large public park including children's play areas, native shrubbery, rose gardens, a landscaped waterway, and is home to the Blenheim Golf Club and its 9-hole course, the Marlborough Tennis club and its courts, and Blenheim Croquet Club. They are dry and arid ranges which have previously been the site of severe grass fires.

The [GCSB Waihopai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCSB_Waihopai "GCSB Waihopai") communications monitoring facility, part of the [ECHELON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECHELON "ECHELON") network, is near Blenheim.

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Transport")]

### Air

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Air")]

[Woodbourne Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbourne_Airport "Woodbourne Airport") is a [domestic airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_airport "Domestic airport") and an [RNZAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_New_Zealand_Air_Force "Royal New Zealand Air Force") operational base. There are direct flights from [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland") and [Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington "Wellington") with [Air New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_New_Zealand "Air New Zealand") and from [Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington "Wellington"), [Christchurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch "Christchurch"), and [Paraparaumu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraparaumu "Paraparaumu") with [Sounds Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sounds_Air "Sounds Air").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-30)

[Omaka Aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaka_Aerodrome "Omaka Aerodrome"), to the south of the town centre, is used solely by private and vintage aircraft. The [Classic Fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Fighters "Classic Fighters") airshow (based mainly on World War I and II aircraft) is held biennially at Easter.

### Road

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Road")]

[State Highway 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_State_Highway_1 "New Zealand State Highway 1") runs through Blenheim and [State Highway 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Highway_6_(New_Zealand) "State Highway 6 (New Zealand)") terminates at the junction of the two state highways. Blenheim is notable for a town of its size in that it does not have [traffic lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_light "Traffic light") at any intersection.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-31) Instead, [roundabouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundabout "Roundabout") speed arterial traffic flow. Since the installation of roundabouts traffic volumes have quickly increased and upgrading options are being considered, e.g. traffic lights, longer two-lane approaches and even a bypass.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-32)

### Rail

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Rail")]

Blenheim is on the [Main North Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_North_Line,_New_Zealand "Main North Line, New Zealand"), the northern part of the unofficially-named [South Island Main Trunk Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island_Main_Trunk_Railway "South Island Main Trunk Railway"). The [Coastal Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_Pacific "Coastal Pacific"), a long-distance passenger train between Picton and Christchurch, stops at [Blenheim railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim_railway_station "Blenheim railway station").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-33) The 1906 station has been listed [NZHPT Category II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_New_Zealand#The_Register "Heritage New Zealand") since 1982.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-34) It is a [standard Vintage station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Troup_(architect)#Standard_Station_designs "George Troup (architect)"), with Tudor half-timbering and tile.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-35)

A major rail freight facility is north of Blenheim at [Spring Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_Creek,_New_Zealand "Spring Creek, New Zealand").

The narrow-gauge [Blenheim Riverside Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim_Riverside_Railway "Blenheim Riverside Railway") runs through the town.

## Infrastructure and services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Infrastructure and services")]

### Electricity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Electricity")]

The Marlborough Electric Power Board (MEPB) was formed in October 1923 and established the Blenheim's first public supply in April 1927, following the commissioning of the Waihopai hydroelectric power station 40 km southwest of Blenheim. Two diesel generators were commissioned at Springlands in 1930 and 1937 to supplement the supply from Waihopai. The town was connected to [Cobb Power Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobb_Power_Station "Cobb Power Station") in 1945,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-36) which in turn was connected to the rest of the South Island grid in 1956. The diesel generators were relegated to standby duty, last generated power on 22 July 1992, and were decommissioned in 2003. The Energy Companies Act 1992 saw the MEPB corporatised and renamed Marlborough Electric. The 1998 electricity sector reforms required electricity companies to separate their lines and supply businesses. Marlborough Electric sold its generation and retailing business to [Trustpower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustpower "Trustpower"), with the remaining lines business renamed [Marlborough Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Lines_Limited "Marlborough Lines Limited").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-37)

Today, Marlborough Lines owns and operates the electricity distribution network servicing the town, with electricity fed from [Transpower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpower_New_Zealand_Limited "Transpower New Zealand Limited")'s national grid at its Blenheim substation in Springlands.

### Water supply and sanitation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Water supply and sanitation")]

Blenheim's water supply is drawn from the Wairau aquifer via nine bores and is treated at two plants in Middle Renwick Road and Bomford Street.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-38)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Education")]

The first school opened in 1859. By 1875 there were three classes: Blenheim Upper Boys', Blenheim Lower Boys', and Blenheim Girls' and Infants'. Blenheim High School was formed within the school in 1879.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-39)

Catholic schools for boys and girls were established in 1872, replaced by St Mary's Boys' School in 1886. In 1929 St Mary's was rebuilt after a fire.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-40)

Marlborough High School, a coeducational secondary school, was founded in Blenheim in 1900. In 1919 it changed its name to Marlborough College. The intermediate section was split to form Bohally Intermediate in 1956. The college was split into separate boys' and girls' schools in 1963, with Marlborough Boys' College (MBC) retaining the existing site and Marlborough Girls' College (MGC) moving to a new site.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-41) An intention to relocate both Marlborough Boys' College and Marlborough Girls' College on the site currently occupied by MGC and Bohally Intermediate was announced in 2019, with Bohally Intermediate relocating to the current MBC site on Stephenson Street.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-42) The relocation plan was scrapped in 2024.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-43)

There are currently 11 schools in the Blenheim urban area: [[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-NZ_school_roll_data-44)

*   **Blenheim School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) primary school. It has a roll of approximately 144.
*   **Bohally Intermediate** is a state intermediate (Year 7–8) school opened in 1957 following a split from Marlborough College. It has a roll of approximately 532.
*   **[Marlborough Boys' College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Boys'_College "Marlborough Boys' College")** is a state boys' secondary (Year 9–13) school. It opened in 1963 following the split of Marlborough College into separate boys' and girls schools, and has a roll of approximately 1,024.
*   **[Marlborough Girls' College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Girls'_College "Marlborough Girls' College")** is a state girls' secondary (Year 9–13) school. It opened in 1963 following the split of Marlborough College into separate boys' and girls school, and has a roll of approximately 960.
*   **Mayfield School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) school in [Mayfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfield,_Blenheim "Mayfield, Blenheim"). It has a roll of approximately 97.
*   **Redwoodtown School** is a state full primary (Year 1–8) school in [Redwoodtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redwoodtown "Redwoodtown"). It has a roll of approximately 308.
*   **Richmond View School** is a state-integrated Christian composite (Year 1–13) school in Redwoodtown. It has a roll of approximately 330.
*   **Springlands School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) school in [Springlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springlands "Springlands"). It has a roll of approximately 350.
*   **St Mary's School** is a state-integrated Catholic full primary (Years 1–8) school. It has a roll of approximately 171.
*   **Whitney Street School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) primary school. It has a roll of approximately 369.
*   **Witherlea School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) primary school in [Witherlea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witherlea "Witherlea"). It has a roll of approximately 388.

Other primary schools are in the surrounding localities of [Renwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renwick,_New_Zealand "Renwick, New Zealand"), [Fairhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairhall "Fairhall"), [Grovetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grovetown,_New_Zealand "Grovetown, New Zealand"), [Rapaura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapaura "Rapaura") and [Riverlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverlands "Riverlands").

The [Nelson Marlborough Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Marlborough_Institute_of_Technology "Nelson Marlborough Institute of Technology") has a campus in Blenheim.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-45)

## Media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Media")]

### Print

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Print")]

Blenheim is served by a variety of print publications. The major daily newspaper serving the area is _[The Marlborough Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Marlborough\_Express "The Marlborough Express")_ published by Fairfax NZ, with its headquarters in Blenheim. _The Saturday Express_ and _Midweek_ are community newspapers published by the same company and distributed throughout Marlborough. _The Blenheim Sun_ is a twice-weekly free newspaper distributed each Wednesday and Friday while the locally owned _Marlborough Weekly_ is published every Tuesday and delivered to every home in the region.

### Radio

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Radio")]

Blenheim is [served by 22 FM radio stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_radio_stations_in_Marlborough "List of radio stations in Marlborough"). The town can also receive AM and FM radio stations from Wellington, due to the straight line-of-sight across Cook Strait and the high power of the transmitters.

**Blenheim** ([/ˈ b l ɛ n ɪ m/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_BLEN-im_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_language "Māori language"): _Waiharakeke_[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-2)) is the most populous [town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town "Town") in the [region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_New_Zealand "Regions of New Zealand") of [Marlborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_District "Marlborough District"), in the north east of the [South Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island "South Island") of [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"). It has an estimated population of 29,800 as of June 2025.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-NZ_population_data_2018-1) The surrounding [Marlborough wine region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_wine_region "Marlborough wine region") is well known as the centre of the [New Zealand wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_wine "New Zealand wine") industry. It enjoys one of New Zealand's sunniest [climates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate "Climate"), with warm, relatively dry summers and cool, crisp winters.

Blenheim is named after the [Battle of Blenheim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Blenheim "Battle of Blenheim") (1704) in the [War of the Spanish Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession "War of the Spanish Succession"), where troops led by [John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Churchill,_1st_Duke_of_Marlborough "John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough") defeated a combined French and [Bavarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria "Bavaria") force. The New Zealand [Ministry for Culture and Heritage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_for_Culture_and_Heritage "Ministry for Culture and Heritage") gives a translation of "[flax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phormium_tenax "Phormium tenax") stream" for the town's Māori name, _Waiharakeke_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Wikipedia-blenheim.jpg/250px-Wikipedia-blenheim.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikipedia-blenheim.jpg)

"Kia Ora Welcome to Blenheim"

The sheltered coastal bays of Marlborough supported a small [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people "Māori people") population possibly as early as the 12th century. Archaeological evidence dates Polynesian human remains uncovered at Wairau Bar to the 13th century. The rich sea and bird life of the area would easily have supported such small communities. As the Māori population of the area increased, they developed the land to sustain the growing population. In the early 1700s canals and waterways were dug among the natural river courses, allowing for the first forms of farming in the area including that of fish and native water fowl. A total of approximately 18 km of channels are known to have been excavated before the arrival of European settlers. Māori in the Marlborough Region also cultivated crops, including kūmara ([sweet potato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_potato "Sweet potato")).

The area is also home to the first serious clash of arms between Māori and the British settlers after the signing of the [Treaty of Waitangi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Waitangi "Treaty of Waitangi"). The [Wairau Affray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wairau_Affray "Wairau Affray") which occurred in what is now the village of [Tuamarina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuamarina "Tuamarina").

The settlement was originally known to Europeans as _The Beaver_ or _Beaverton_[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-4) due to its frequent flooding.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-5)

Although the early history of Marlborough was closely associated with the [Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Province "Nelson Province") settlement, the people of Marlborough desired independence from Nelson. In 1859, nineteen years after the original Nelson settlement, the request of Marlborough settlers was granted, and Marlborough became a [separate province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Province "Marlborough Province"). Although gold was discovered in the province in the early 1860s the resulting boom did not last, and while the gold rush helped to expand the region, it was the development of pastoralism which provided the greatest long-term benefits. Marlborough squatters developed huge sheep runs that dominated the countryside, rivalling [Canterbury's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury,_New_Zealand "Canterbury, New Zealand") sheep stations in size and wealth.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Blenheim_New_Zeland.jpg/250px-Blenheim_New_Zeland.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blenheim_New_Zeland.jpg)

View from above looking north from Blenheim

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Blenheim%2C_NZ.jpg/250px-Blenheim%2C_NZ.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blenheim,_NZ.jpg)

The Taylor River in central Blenheim

Situated on the Wairau Plain, the town is mostly flat with only its southernmost fringe rising to the base of the Wither Hills. As the plain is surrounded by mountains on all but the eastern flank, which is open to Cook Strait, it is relatively well protected from the frequent southerly weather fronts occurring during winters. The area does however experience some high wind events during the course of the year, especially from the west where the wind is funnelled down the [Wairau Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wairau_Valley "Wairau Valley") directly at the town. Open and exposed areas in and around Blenheim are also hit quite hard by winds blowing inland from Cook Strait. Blenheim sits at the confluence of the [Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_River_(Marlborough,_New_Zealand) "Taylor River (Marlborough, New Zealand)") and [Ōpaoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Cpaoa_River "Ōpaoa River") rivers. It is in a tectonically active zone and experiences several (usually small) earthquakes each year. The boundary between the Pacific plate (on which Blenheim sits) and the Indo-Australian plate passes just north of Blenheim. It lies east of Renwick, and just south of Spring Creek.

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Climate")]

The climate is generally very settled, largely due to the [rain shadow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_shadow "Rain shadow") effect of the mountain ranges to the west which [shelter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foehn_effect "Foehn effect") Blenheim from the heaviest of rains that hit the western part of the South Island.

Summers are typically warm, dry and sunny. Winter mornings are cool and frosty. Snowfall is rare as the town is sheltered from cold southerly weather by the mountain ranges to the south. Rainfall and humidity is highest in winter and early spring, between June and October. The town's average annual rainfall is a little more than 700mm, with 81.5 precipitation days.

Thunderstorms are an uncommon occurrence due to the sheltered climate. There is a higher likelihood in summer, when afternoon heating can generate a buildup of clouds above the ranges.

The highest recorded temperature is 37.8°C, recorded on 7 February 1973.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-6) The lowest is −8.8°C.

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Economy")]

The town's economy is based on agricultural services, with [pastoral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoral "Pastoral") and [horticultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horticultural "Horticultural") farming providing a major source of income. Historically, sheep farming, dairying, and wheat and barley were the major activities in the area. Marlborough's first commercial grape vines were planted in 1973, and since then [viticulture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viticulture "Viticulture") has become the dominant industry in the region; employment is derived not only from the production of wine, but also from 'wine tourism' in the area. [Olive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive "Olive") growing has also gained some importance in recent years. Despite being located several kilometres inland, maritime industries are also important sources of employment for Blenheim. [Lake Grassmere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Grassmere "Lake Grassmere") has New Zealand's only [salt works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt "Salt"), producing 50% of the country's total salt requirement. [Fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing "Fishing") and [mussel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mussel "Mussel") farming are also important in the region.

### Wine production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Wine production")]

Main article: [Marlborough wine region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_wine_region "Marlborough wine region")

Viticulture also has a very large impact on the local economy both directly, by way of employment and servicing required, and also by way of 'wine tourism'. The local cellars attracted hundreds of thousands of domestic and international tourists every year. The area also hosts the annual [Marlborough Wine & Food Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Wine_&_Food_Festival?action=edit&redlink=1 "Marlborough Wine & Food Festival (page does not exist)"). The [Marlborough wine region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_wine_region "Marlborough wine region") is now New Zealand's largest, and receives worldwide recognition for its [Sauvignon Blanc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauvignon_Blanc "Sauvignon Blanc") wines.

With its growing international critical recognition, much of the Marlborough wine industry has come to be dominated by large firms, owned by major New Zealand companies or offshore investors. There are over 50 vineyards near Blenheim. Agricultural land prices in the [Wairau Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wairau_Valley "Wairau Valley") increased dramatically in the 1990s and 2000s.

## Lifestyle

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Lifestyle")]

The sunny, pleasant [climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate "Climate") has long attracted people to the region, as holiday-makers or as permanent [settlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlers "Settlers"). The region is especially popular among retired people, as well as people seeking an alternative lifestyle. Rapid population growth and other factors though have led to a contemporary chronic shortage of affordable housing for low and middle income earners.

The Marlborough Region has a wide range of predominantly outdoor [leisure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leisure "Leisure") activities and the relaxed lifestyle and the flourishing wine and [gourmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gourmet "Gourmet") food industry in Marlborough are enjoyed by both locals and visitors alike.

[Omaka Aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaka_Aerodrome "Omaka Aerodrome"), south of the town centre, is the setting for the two-yearly [Classic Fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Fighters "Classic Fighters") Marlborough airshow. With a large emphasis on aircraft of World War One, it has been held since 2001.

Seymour Square and Pollard Park are two of the town centres main attractions for walks and general tourism. Seymour Square is an open public area in the centre, containing the War Memorial and Clock Tower, unveiled in 1928, classified as a "Category I" ("places of 'special or outstanding historical or cultural heritage significance or value'") historic place by [Heritage New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_New_Zealand "Heritage New Zealand").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-28) The Square was named after Henry Seymour.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-29) Pollard Park is a large public park including children's play areas, native shrubbery, rose gardens, a landscaped waterway, and is home to the Blenheim Golf Club and its 9-hole course, the Marlborough Tennis club and its courts, and Blenheim Croquet Club. They are dry and arid ranges which have previously been the site of severe grass fires.

The [GCSB Waihopai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCSB_Waihopai "GCSB Waihopai") communications monitoring facility, part of the [ECHELON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECHELON "ECHELON") network, is near Blenheim.

## Transport

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Transport")]

### Air

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Air")]

[Woodbourne Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbourne_Airport "Woodbourne Airport") is a [domestic airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_airport "Domestic airport") and an [RNZAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_New_Zealand_Air_Force "Royal New Zealand Air Force") operational base. There are direct flights from [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland") and [Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington "Wellington") with [Air New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_New_Zealand "Air New Zealand") and from [Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington "Wellington"), [Christchurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch "Christchurch"), and [Paraparaumu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraparaumu "Paraparaumu") with [Sounds Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sounds_Air "Sounds Air").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-30)

[Omaka Aerodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaka_Aerodrome "Omaka Aerodrome"), to the south of the town centre, is used solely by private and vintage aircraft. The [Classic Fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_Fighters "Classic Fighters") airshow (based mainly on World War I and II aircraft) is held biennially at Easter.

### Road

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Road")]

[State Highway 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_State_Highway_1 "New Zealand State Highway 1") runs through Blenheim and [State Highway 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Highway_6_(New_Zealand) "State Highway 6 (New Zealand)") terminates at the junction of the two state highways. Blenheim is notable for a town of its size in that it does not have [traffic lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_light "Traffic light") at any intersection.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-31) Instead, [roundabouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundabout "Roundabout") speed arterial traffic flow. Since the installation of roundabouts traffic volumes have quickly increased and upgrading options are being considered, e.g. traffic lights, longer two-lane approaches and even a bypass.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-32)

### Rail

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Rail")]

Blenheim is on the [Main North Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_North_Line,_New_Zealand "Main North Line, New Zealand"), the northern part of the unofficially-named [South Island Main Trunk Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island_Main_Trunk_Railway "South Island Main Trunk Railway"). The [Coastal Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_Pacific "Coastal Pacific"), a long-distance passenger train between Picton and Christchurch, stops at [Blenheim railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim_railway_station "Blenheim railway station").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-33) The 1906 station has been listed [NZHPT Category II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_New_Zealand#The_Register "Heritage New Zealand") since 1982.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-34) It is a [standard Vintage station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Troup_(architect)#Standard_Station_designs "George Troup (architect)"), with Tudor half-timbering and tile.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-35)

A major rail freight facility is north of Blenheim at [Spring Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_Creek,_New_Zealand "Spring Creek, New Zealand").

The narrow-gauge [Blenheim Riverside Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim_Riverside_Railway "Blenheim Riverside Railway") runs through the town.

## Infrastructure and services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Infrastructure and services")]

### Electricity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Electricity")]

The Marlborough Electric Power Board (MEPB) was formed in October 1923 and established the Blenheim's first public supply in April 1927, following the commissioning of the Waihopai hydroelectric power station 40 km southwest of Blenheim. Two diesel generators were commissioned at Springlands in 1930 and 1937 to supplement the supply from Waihopai. The town was connected to [Cobb Power Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cobb_Power_Station "Cobb Power Station") in 1945,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-36) which in turn was connected to the rest of the South Island grid in 1956. The diesel generators were relegated to standby duty, last generated power on 22 July 1992, and were decommissioned in 2003. The Energy Companies Act 1992 saw the MEPB corporatised and renamed Marlborough Electric. The 1998 electricity sector reforms required electricity companies to separate their lines and supply businesses. Marlborough Electric sold its generation and retailing business to [Trustpower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trustpower "Trustpower"), with the remaining lines business renamed [Marlborough Lines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Lines_Limited "Marlborough Lines Limited").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-37)

Today, Marlborough Lines owns and operates the electricity distribution network servicing the town, with electricity fed from [Transpower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transpower_New_Zealand_Limited "Transpower New Zealand Limited")'s national grid at its Blenheim substation in Springlands.

### Water supply and sanitation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Water supply and sanitation")]

Blenheim's water supply is drawn from the Wairau aquifer via nine bores and is treated at two plants in Middle Renwick Road and Bomford Street.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-38)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Education")]

The first school opened in 1859. By 1875 there were three classes: Blenheim Upper Boys', Blenheim Lower Boys', and Blenheim Girls' and Infants'. Blenheim High School was formed within the school in 1879.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-39)

Catholic schools for boys and girls were established in 1872, replaced by St Mary's Boys' School in 1886. In 1929 St Mary's was rebuilt after a fire.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-40)

Marlborough High School, a coeducational secondary school, was founded in Blenheim in 1900. In 1919 it changed its name to Marlborough College. The intermediate section was split to form Bohally Intermediate in 1956. The college was split into separate boys' and girls' schools in 1963, with Marlborough Boys' College (MBC) retaining the existing site and Marlborough Girls' College (MGC) moving to a new site.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-41) An intention to relocate both Marlborough Boys' College and Marlborough Girls' College on the site currently occupied by MGC and Bohally Intermediate was announced in 2019, with Bohally Intermediate relocating to the current MBC site on Stephenson Street.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-42) The relocation plan was scrapped in 2024.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-43)

There are currently 11 schools in the Blenheim urban area: [[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-NZ_school_roll_data-44)

*   **Blenheim School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) primary school. It has a roll of approximately 144.
*   **Bohally Intermediate** is a state intermediate (Year 7–8) school opened in 1957 following a split from Marlborough College. It has a roll of approximately 532.
*   **[Marlborough Boys' College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Boys'_College "Marlborough Boys' College")** is a state boys' secondary (Year 9–13) school. It opened in 1963 following the split of Marlborough College into separate boys' and girls schools, and has a roll of approximately 1,024.
*   **[Marlborough Girls' College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlborough_Girls'_College "Marlborough Girls' College")** is a state girls' secondary (Year 9–13) school. It opened in 1963 following the split of Marlborough College into separate boys' and girls school, and has a roll of approximately 960.
*   **Mayfield School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) school in [Mayfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfield,_Blenheim "Mayfield, Blenheim"). It has a roll of approximately 97.
*   **Redwoodtown School** is a state full primary (Year 1–8) school in [Redwoodtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redwoodtown "Redwoodtown"). It has a roll of approximately 308.
*   **Richmond View School** is a state-integrated Christian composite (Year 1–13) school in Redwoodtown. It has a roll of approximately 330.
*   **Springlands School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) school in [Springlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springlands "Springlands"). It has a roll of approximately 350.
*   **St Mary's School** is a state-integrated Catholic full primary (Years 1–8) school. It has a roll of approximately 171.
*   **Whitney Street School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) primary school. It has a roll of approximately 369.
*   **Witherlea School** is a state contributing primary (Year 1–6) primary school in [Witherlea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witherlea "Witherlea"). It has a roll of approximately 388.

Other primary schools are in the surrounding localities of [Renwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renwick,_New_Zealand "Renwick, New Zealand"), [Fairhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairhall "Fairhall"), [Grovetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grovetown,_New_Zealand "Grovetown, New Zealand"), [Rapaura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapaura "Rapaura") and [Riverlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverlands "Riverlands").

The [Nelson Marlborough Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Marlborough_Institute_of_Technology "Nelson Marlborough Institute of Technology") has a campus in Blenheim.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blenheim,_New_Zealand#cite_note-45)

## Media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Media")]

### Print

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Print")]

Blenheim is served by a variety of print publications. The major daily newspaper serving the area is _[The Marlborough Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Marlborough\_Express "The Marlborough Express")_ published by Fairfax NZ, with its headquarters in Blenheim. _The Saturday Express_ and _Midweek_ are community newspapers published by the same company and distributed throughout Marlborough. _The Blenheim Sun_ is a twice-weekly free newspaper distributed each Wednesday and Friday while the locally owned _Marlborough Weekly_ is published every Tuesday and delivered to every home in the region.

### Radio

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blenheim,_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Radio")]

Blenheim is [served by 22 FM radio stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_radio_stations_in_Marlborough "List of radio stations in Marlborough"). The town can also receive AM and FM radio stations from Wellington, due to the straight line-of-sight across Cook Strait and the high power of the transmitters.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Statistical areas in New Zealand

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/NewZealandPopulationDensity.png/250px-NewZealandPopulationDensity.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NewZealandPopulationDensity.png)

Urban areas correspond to the more [densely populated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") areas of New Zealand: 

100 people per square km and above

250 people per square km and above

500 people per square km and above

750 people per square km and above

1000 people per square km and above

2000 people per square km and above

3000 people per square km and above

4000 people per square km and above

[Statistics New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_New_Zealand "Statistics New Zealand") defines **urban areas of New Zealand** for statistical purposes (they have no administrative or legal basis).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-defn-1) The [urban areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area") comprise [cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cities_in_New_Zealand "Cities in New Zealand"), [towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_towns_in_New_Zealand "List of towns in New Zealand") and other [conurbations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conurbation "Conurbation") (an aggregation of urban settlements) of a thousand people or more. In combination they constitute [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand")'s urban population,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-defn-1) which makes up 84.5% of New Zealand's total population, as of June 2025.

The current standard for urban areas is the Statistical Standard for Geographic Areas 2023 (SSGA23), an update of SSGA18, which had replaced the New Zealand Standard Areas Classification 1992 (NZSAC92) in 2018.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-SSGA23-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-stats.govt.nz-3) There are four classes of urban area under SSGA23 and SSGA18 – major, large, medium and small. Each urban area consists of one or more level-2 statistical areas (SA2s). Urban areas under SSGA18 do not cross territorial authority boundaries, with one exception ([Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_New_Zealand "Richmond, New Zealand"), which lies in the [Tasman District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasman_District "Tasman District") but includes the Daelyn SA2 area from neighbouring Nelson City).

Under SSGA18, details of the four classes were:

*   Major urban areas have a population of 100,000 or more. There are seven of them, with a combined population of 2,734,900 (51.4% of the total population).
*   Large urban areas have a population of 30,000 to 99,999. There are 13 of them, with a combined population of 727,300 (13.7% of the total population).
*   Medium urban areas have a population of 10,000 to 29,999. There are 23 of them, with a combined population of 482,500 (9.1% of the total population).
*   Small urban areas have a population of 1,000 to 9,999. There are 152 of them, with a combined population of 556,900 (10.5% of the total population).

Statistics New Zealand also defines rural settlements with a population of 200 to 999 people or at least 40 dwellings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-review2021-4) While these do not fit the standard international definition of an urban population, they serve to distinguish between true rural dwellers and those in rural settlements or towns. There are 402 rural settlements which combined have a population of 157,800 (3.0% of the total population).

While SSGA23 is similar to SSGA18, it added a new geographical area (SA3), upgraded Wānaka to a medium urban area, upgraded seven rural settlements to small urban areas, and created thirteen new rural settlements.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-2023_Stats_NZ_datafinder-5)

## New Zealand Standard Areas Classification 1992

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: New Zealand Standard Areas Classification 1992")]

Under the New Zealand Standard Areas Classification 1992 (NZSAC92), there are three classes of urban area:[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-urban_area-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand#cite_note-geo_defs-9)

*   Main urban areas, with a population of 30,000 or more. These 17 areas mostly correspond to the places known by New Zealanders as cities.
*   Secondary urban areas are the 14 urban areas with a population of 10,000 to 29,999.
*   Minor urban areas make up the remainder of the urban population of the country, towns with 1,000 to 9,999 people. There are 103 minor urban areas.

### Main urban areas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Urban_areas_of_New_Zealand&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Main urban areas")]

1992
Original classification

1996
No change

2001
*   Kapiti promoted from secondary to main urban area
*   Rolleston added as minor urban area
*   Pauanui Beach dropped to rural centre

2006
*   Edgecumbe Community renamed Edgecumbe

2013
*   Blenheim promoted from secondary to main urban area
*   Rangiora and Queenstown promoted from minor to secondary urban areas
*   Gore demoted from secondary to minor urban area
*   Ngunguru, Mangawhai Heads, Te Kauwhata, Ngatea, Mapua, Amberley, Methven, Rakaia and Waikouaiti added as minor urban areas
